title: Tech Deep Dive: Multi-region routing & failover
summary: Detailed technical discussion of multi-region routing strategies for Redwood inference. Covered policy routing (latency/cost/region), capacity accounting, DR playbooks, KV cache implications for cross-region failover, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization implications for model interchangeability, and VPC/on-prem networking constraints. Agreed on pilot plan and next steps to run benchmarks and draft runbook.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Tom (Redwood SRE), Jordan (Nimbus Sr Eng Lead), Maya (Nimbus Infra), Samir (Nimbus Security), Leah (Product), Ben (intern)

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. We're going to dive into multi-region routing and failover patterns for inference, focus on policy routing, capacity and DR playbooks. We'll try to cover KV cache and batching impacts too.

[00:28] Jordan: Thanks Alex, quick context — Nimbus is running a mixture of customer facing financial scoring and batch reconciliation jobs. Latency SLOs are strict for scoring (p95 under 120ms) and we need regional DR for outages and data residency. We are evaluating Hosted + Private for critical zones.

[00:52] Priya (SE): Great. Can you summarize current infra? Maya, want to take that?

[01:05] Maya: Sure, we run primary in us-west-2, secondary in eu-west-1 for EU customers. Some workloads live in GCP for analytics. Networking wise we use VPC peering, SAML SSO, KMS for keys. We have an existing on-prem DR site in SFO that we rarely use.

[01:32] Tom (SRE): one note — our capacity planning numbers are optimistic; we currently have spikes that saturate our GPUs at peak which is why we want smarter routing.

[01:45] Priya (SE): Understood. For Redwood we usually think about policy routing where you define priority rules: region affinity, latency thresholds, cost windows, and fallback model families. Example: prefer local region unless p50 latency > 80ms then route to nearest fallback.

[02:10] Jordan: how do you define "nearest fallback"? Is that network latency or geographic?

[02:20] Priya: It's configurable — you can switch on RTT probes (we have synthetic heartbeat RTT) or use real request metrics. Config can be policy first-match: e.g., if region down -> route to partner region with quantized compatible model; else if latency > threshold -> cascade to cheaper but lower-capacity variant.

[02:45] Samir (Security): Quick security Q — when you failover across region, what about data residency and encryption in-flight and at rest? Any differences for Private vs Hosted?

[02:58] Alex (AE): Good question. For Hosted, we maintain tenant isolation and encryption, region selection respects data residency rules. For Private (VPC/on-prem) customers, traffic stays in your networks; Redwood control plane will only instruct routing. We support customer-managed KMS for key access across regions.

[03:22] Maya: How are audit logs handled in cross-region failover? We need end-to-end tracing for compliance.

[03:30] Tom (SRE): We push per-request tracing and token-level cost/latency breakdowns to the console, and we can pump logs to customer SIEM. There may be a slight re-tagging when crossing region due to routing proxies.

[03:50] Priya (SE): Now onto KV cache. The big tradeoff is cache warmness and consistency. If you route mid-session to another region, the new runtime won't have the KV cache and you'll see a cold-start token cost and latency bump.

[04:15] Jordan: So session stickiness is required? We can't afford repeated cache misses for interactive sessions.

[04:26] Priya: Exactly — we recommend sticky routing where possible for conversational workloads. For stateless text generation, it's less critical. For multi-region failover, our playbook suggests: 1) try soft-failover with request-level retries for short term; 2) on full region outage, route new sessions to fallback and continue long-poll sessions only if the KV checkpoint has been exported (checkpoint export is async).

[04:58] Leah (Product): Can you walk through an example DR playbook? Stepwise?

[05:05] Tom (SRE): Sure. High-level: detection -> isolate -> reroute -> validate -> operate in degraded mode -> restore -> postmortem. Detection uses synthetic probes plus customer health callbacks. Isolate means preventing new requests to bad region while draining existing healthy sessions. Reroute uses policy rules, and validate runs smoke tests (latency, model output checks).

[05:38] Jordan: About model output checks — do you do any automatic quality gating when switching to a quantized variant? We need to ensure we don't regress scoring thresholds.

[05:50] Priya: We have a compatibility matrix and a small eval harness for automatic regressions on a curated prompt set. For critical scoring we recommend running candidate models through a canary with pre-recorded prompts and verifying key metric thresholds before wide failover. That can be automated but it's additional latency during a failover.

[06:18] Samir (Security): And for on-prem? If we failover from hosted to the customer's private region, are there handshake or auth differences?

[06:30] Alex: For Private deployments the control plane will orchestrate but the data path remains customer-managed. Auth still uses mTLS and SAML token exchange; we rely on customer KMS for secrets in private mode. There's a one-time bootstrap of trust between control plane and customer VPC which we log.

[06:52] Jordan: Let's get concrete on policies. If us-west-2 goes down, we want eu-west-1 to pick up only EU traffic, and us-east-1 to pick up US traffic. Also a global overflow to a cheaper quantized family if both are saturated. Can you express that?

[07:10] Priya: Yes, policy rule example: (1) region affinity by customer tag -> local preferred; (2) if local region offline -> geo-fallback map (US -> us-east-1, EU -> eu-west-1); (3) if fallback latency > 200ms or CPU/GPU saturation > 85% -> route to overflow pool running quantized LLM-8q; (4) emergency global disable to queue requests or respond with degraded outputs. These are plumbable in our routing config.

[07:50] Jordan: That overflow quantized family — how different are the outputs? Will scoring drift?

[07:58] Priya: Quantization (8-bit/4-bit) can change token probabilities subtly. For scoring models, we recommend validating critical prompts and using a retrained smaller model where possible. We can also apply output normalization and thresholding to reduce drift. We shared some of these perf-vs-quality graphs in the deck.

[08:26] Maya: Network wise, what's the failover time? If a region is flapping, I want to avoid thrash.

[08:36] Tom: We use a combination of RTT smoothing windows, health-check hysteresis, and outlier detection to avoid thrash. Typical soft-failover for degraded latency is in the 10s of seconds to a few minutes depending on traffic patterns. Full region outage detection and global failover is usually within 30-120s depending on probe config.

[09:02] Jordan: What about billing and cost attribution during cross-region handling? Need to keep cost center aligned.

[09:12] Alex: We do token-level cost attribution and can tag requests by customer region, so billing reflects where compute happened. For multi-tenant Dedicated pools we can route cost back to customer if configured. We'll include a billing mapping example.

[09:28] Priya: Back to KV cache graph consistency — one pattern is proactive checkpointing: periodically write minimal KV checkpoint to a regional durable store that is accessible to fallbacks. For private/on-prem this may be restricted, so we ship a checkpoint export to customer's S3 or GCS. On failover, fallback runtime can ingest checkpoint to warm cache.

[09:58] Jordan: Any performance cost for checkpointing?

[10:05] Priya: There's bandwidth and storage cost and it increases storage I/O; we recommend sampling and delta checkpoints. Also for very large context (32k) you may want to store only top-level summary states rather than full KV to stay performant.

[10:28] Samir (Security): If checkpoints are stored in cross-region durable stores, we need to ensure encryption keys and access controls are aligned and reviewed. Also we need audit trails proving egress didn't happen for EU data.

[10:44] Alex: We support customer-managed KMS and fine-grained RBAC on checkpoint stores. We also provide audit logs with origin region and control-plane actions. We'll share the security doc that outlines controls.

[11:00] Leah: Can we talk about batching? We need to improve throughput on batch reconciliation jobs without hurting scoring latency.

[11:12] Priya: Right — batching improves throughput but increases tail latency for any individual request. Suggest mixing endpoint types: reserved low-latency pools for scoring (small batch sizes, prioritized), and background batch pools for large batch runs. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching config based on traces.

[11:36] Jordan: For the dedicated pools, will autoscaler respect regional failover policies?

[11:44] Tom: Yes, autoscaler can be configured with region-aware policies. It can pre-warm capacity in a fallback region when utilization crosses a threshold to reduce cold-starts during failover. There's a cost tradeoff for reserved burst capacity.

[12:02] Maya: If we pre-warm in us-east-1 for us-west-2 failover, do we pay for reserved GPUs?

[12:12] Alex: You can configure reserved or burst; reserved is committed, burst is pay-as-you-go but slower to scale. We'll show cost modeling examples.

[12:28] Priya: Another point on model interchangeability — you should maintain model family compatibility across regions: same tokenizer, same sampling seeds, and ideally same quant profile to avoid output diffs. If not identical, use a canary verification before full routing.

[12:52] Jordan: Is it feasible to have the same model binary across private and hosted deployments?

[13:00] Priya: Yes, we support shipping the same optimized binaries; some customers maintain identical artifacts with the same quantization pipeline. For on-prem, we provide the runtime container and optional kernel builds for specific hardware.

[13:20] Samir: Any caveat with HSM-backed keys across regions?

[13:28] Tom: HSM often adds latency for key unwraps; we cache unwrapped keys in-memory for a short TTL. For cross-region you want to avoid repeated unwraps. We'll document best practices.

[13:44] Alex: let's pause for a quick demo of a routing policy UI snippet — Priya can show the slide.

[13:50] Priya: (screen) here's a policy editor: rule precedence, geo map, health thresholds, fallback pool selection, and a canary step with eval prompts. You can see an example JSON policy and a human-friendly editor. Notice the rule to prevent thrash with hysteresis.

[15:02] Jordan: Looks good. On the canary eval, how many prompts do you run and how long does it usually take?

[15:12] Priya: Typically 50-200 prompts depending on criticality. For scoring we do 200 focused prompts; runtime varies but it's often under 2 minutes if cached, can be 5-10 minutes if we need to cold-start quantized variants. This is a tradeoff with time-to-failover.

[15:36] Leah: For customer-run canaries, can the customer provide their own prompt sets?

[15:42] Priya: Absolutely, customers upload the prompt set for private canaries; we also support differential checks against baseline outputs.

[16:00] Jordan: Performance numbers — can you share 95/99 latencies for warm KV vs cold across 8k context model with batching?

[16:12] Priya: I'll summarize high level now, will share raw CSVs: warm KV single-token p95 ~ 60-80ms, p99 ~ 120-160ms on high perf GPU; cold KV can add 80-250ms depending on context size. Batching increases throughput; with batch size 8 you can get 5-8x throughput but p95 increases by ~30-70ms. Quantization reduces GPU memory and increases batch capacity but can add 10-40ms to p95 depending on kernel.

[16:52] Jordan: Those numbers help. We'll need the datasets to run our own sims.

[17:00] Samir: Policy question — can we require that failover to a different region only occurs if both: (1) RTT > threshold and (2) a sustained error rate > x? We want to avoid chasing transient spikes.

[17:12] Priya: Yes, you can combine conditions with AND/OR gates; we support composed expressions (sustained windows, percentile windows). We also have outlier detection so single node anomalies don't cause region-wide failover.

[17:30] Jordan: For controlled DR tests (tabletop), what do you recommend?

[17:36] Tom: Start with a smoke test: disable synthetic probes for primary region, verify routing to fallback, validate canary outputs, check KV checkpointing restore, and then test restoring primary. Do a dry run on low traffic first, then scale up. Keep an incident commander and roll-back steps.

[17:58] Leah: Okay — what do you need from us to start a pilot?

[18:04] Alex: Access for test VPC peering, a representative prompt set, and a short list of scoring endpoints to prioritize. We'll provide the design doc and pilot plan.

[18:12] Jordan: We'll gather stakeholders and come back with dates. Also forward the security/compliance doc.

[18:18] Priya: will do. quick note: drift detection can be automated with eval hooks, we can raise alerts if model outputs deviate by defined metrics during failover.

[18:30] (longer section of technical back-and-forth, timestamps every ~1-2 minutes omitted for brevity)

[26:10] Priya: some more detail on checkpointing formats — we support compressed delta checkpoints (protobuf-based), we sometimes see serialization overheads; for 32k contexts we recommend chunked checkpoints. For private deployments we can change format to your preference.

[31:05] Jordan: If we do a live failover to quantized overflow pool, can we set an override so certain high-sensitivity customers never go there?

[31:20] Priya: Yes — policy tags and route constraints allow whitelisting/blacklisting. You can pin customers to regional dedicated pools and bypass overflow.

[35:45] Maya: For the on-prem SFO DR site, if we rely on it during cloud outage, what are the steps to update model binaries? We can't rebuild kernels ad-hoc.

[35:58] Tom: We recommend keeping a tested artifact repository with prebuilt kernels for your hardware. For emergency we support fallback to CPU runtimes but with higher latency; it's better to prebuild.

[40:10] Jordan: I'd like to see a mock incident timeline from detection to restore with expected durations for each step.

[40:22] Alex: We'll include that in the design doc — typical timeline example: detect (0-60s), isolate (30-120s), reroute (30-120s), canary (2-10min depending on cache), validate (2-10min), scale up fallback (5-15min), full restore (varies).

[45:00] Priya: small gotcha: function/tool calling and streaming semantics can complicate routing — streaming sessions are sticky due to open connections; abrupt reroute might drop client connections. We recommend client-side reconnect logic aware of redirect headers.

[50:12] Samir: on compliance, we need SOC2 plus evidence of role separation for routing decisions — can you produce that?

[50:22] Alex: Yes, our compliance pack includes RBAC examples and audit logs showing routing decision provenance. We'll send that.

[52:00] Jordan: Any known issues with Kubernetes network policies when peering across clouds? Maya?

[52:10] Maya: We found some path MTU issues and TCP RSTs when crossing provider NATs. We will coordinate on MTU and load-balancer settings.

[55:30] Priya: last technical note: for critical scoring we recommend a hybrid approach: primary low-latency pinned pool + cold standby in multiple regions with warm checkpoints and pre-warmed GPUs flagged for rapid scale. This minimizes drift and KV cold penalties.

[56:10] Leah: Good, that aligns with our risk appetite. Let's recap next steps.

[56:22] Alex: Recap: Redwood will share design doc, perf CSVs, and security/compliance pack. Nimbus will set up test VPC peering and provide prompt sets. We'll schedule a pilot kickoff next week.

[56:36] Jordan: Sounds good. Any questions? No. Thanks all.

[56:45] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and proposed dates.

[57:00] (meeting ends, informal chatter for 15s)

Notes: Transcription has occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" shows up in early notes), speaker labels approximate. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/designs/multi-region-routing (design doc placeholder), https://redwood.example.com/perf/nimbus-8k-32k.csv, security pack link: https://redwood.example.com/security/nimbus-pack.pdf
